section_1.title: Introduction: The 'Error' Concept
section_1.content: Define the cost function as a measure of 'how wrong' the neural network is. Introduce the prerequisite of the loss calculation as the difference between predicted output and actual ground truth.
section_1.example: A cat-recognizing neural network guesses a dog; the distance between the 'dog' probability and the 'cat' label is the 'Cost'.

section_2.title: Visualizing the Cost Surface
section_2.content: Represent the cost function as a 3D landscape. High points (peaks) represent high error; low points (valleys) represent accuracy. We want the network to 'roll down' to the lowest point.
section_2.example: Imagine a hiker (the model) standing on a foggy mountain (the cost surface) trying to find the base camp (the global minimum) without seeing the path.

section_3.title: The Mechanism of Gradient Descent
section_3.content: Explain the gradient (derivative) as the 'slope' or 'direction of steepest ascent'. To minimize cost, we move in the negative direction of the gradient. Emphasize that weight updates happen incrementally.
section_3.example: The hiker feels the slope of the ground with their feet and takes a small step downward. This is the weight update step.

section_4.title: Hyperparameters: Step Size and Learning Rate
section_4.content: Introduce the 'learning rate'. If the step is too large, we overshoot the valley; if too small, the process is agonizingly slow.
section_4.example: A hiker taking giant leaps might jump over the valley entirely, while one taking microscopic steps will never reach the camp before sunset.

section_5.title: Conclusion: The Iterative Loop
section_5.content: Synthesize the process: Forward pass (calculate cost) -> Backward pass (calculate gradient) -> Update weights. This cycle is what we call 'Training'.
section_5.example: Like training a puppy: the network makes a mistake, receives feedback (gradient), adjusts its behavior, and repeats until it sits perfectly on command.
